Unordered mean pooling of jointly trained token embeddings provides shared lexical features, but is permutation invariant: it cannot distinguish texts with identical token counts and different number–unit assignments. Any gain could reflect brand, topic, or identifier overlap rather than functional understanding. Local CNNs offer a relevant alternative: Johnson and Zhang learn representations of small text regions directly from supervised data, while Kim includes a randomly initialized, trainable CNN baseline. These establish feasible controls without pretrained language models, although neither establishes recommendation gains. [Johnson and Zhang, 2015](https://aclanthology.org/N15-1011/); [Kim, 2014](https://aclanthology.org/D14-1181/).

A suitable proposed control is one HSTU network with item representation ID embedding + projected text encoding, trained jointly through the recommendation loss. Compare masked mean pooling against a small local CNN while holding tokenization, text limits, fusion, backbone, training budget, and evaluation fixed; retain numeric strings, units, and alphanumeric model identifiers. Separately trained ablations can test shuffled word order and removed numeric/unit/identifier tokens; each evaluated predictor remains one model. These are experimental recommendations, not established findings for this benchmark.

Claims about compatibility or numerical specificity require targeted evidence. Numeracy studies find that embedding capabilities vary by representation and probe; approximate magnitude does not imply reliable numerical equivalence or extrapolation. Consequently, scratch text pooling should be described as lexical sharing unless controlled validation demonstrates more specific behavior. A CNN can preserve local number–unit associations, but does not inherently learn arithmetic, unit conversion, or product compatibility. [Naik et al., 2019](https://aclanthology.org/P19-1329/); [Wallace et al., 2019](https://aclanthology.org/D19-1534/).
